title: the 'Will' sonnet
short: Sonnet 135, addressed to the dark lady, plays on 'will' in many senses, including Shakespeare's own first name.
body: Sonnets 135 and 136 are the 'Will' sonnets, in which the word occurs some twenty times across the pair. The 1609 Quarto capitalizes and italicizes several instances, as it often does with proper names, which suggests the name William; but the Quarto's italics are inconsistent, and editors disagree about which uses are names. The opening varies a proverbial phrase ('Women will have their wills'): other women may have their wish, but you have your Will, both your desire and a man (or men) called Will. 'Hath' may mean 'may have'.

title: the senses of 'will'
short: 'Will' means desire, sexual appetite, the genitals of either sex, the future auxiliary, and the name William.
body: The commentaries lay out overlapping senses: wish or volition; carnal desire; stubborn wilfulness; slang for the penis and the vagina; the auxiliary of the future tense; and the name Will. 'To boot' means in addition and 'over-plus' means surplus, so line 2 implies that the lady has more than one Will: perhaps the poet himself, perhaps the friend (if he too was called William, as some argue for William Herbert), perhaps her husband. The RPO notes gloss 'Will to boot' as William the poet and 'Will in over-plus' as possibly the friend. The ambiguity is deliberate and cannot be fully resolved.

title: vex'd thee still
short: The poet admits he has always ('still') pestered her with his suit.
body: 'Still' has its regular Elizabethan sense of always, continually, as the RPO note glosses it. 'Vex'd' means troubled or annoyed. The speaker presents himself, with self-deprecation, as more than enough, an excess added to her 'sweet will' 'thus', by his very insistence. The mercantile 'addition' continues the language of surplus begun in line 2. 'Addition' was also the word for a title or mark of honour added to a name, so the poet adds his Will to hers as a supplement to her name.

title: whose will is large and spacious
short: Her desire is vast and accommodating, a bawdy hint that she receives many lovers.
body: The phrase plays on 'will' as both appetite and the female sexual organ: the lady's will is wide enough to take in more. The RPO note glosses line 5's 'will' as the vagina and line 6's 'my will' as the penis. The sexual joke is coarse, but the tone is also one of abject pleading: he asks her to 'vouchsafe' (grant, condescend) to admit him once among the rest. 'Gracious' in line 7 means pleasing, favoured, and has a theological ring (in a state of grace).

title: The sea, all water, yet receives rain
short: As the sea, already full, still takes in rain and adds it to its store, so she should take in his will too.
body: The comparison echoes Ecclesiastes 1.7: 'All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full.' Shakespeare uses a similar image of love's capacity in Twelfth Night 1.1, where Orsino's love 'Receiveth as the sea' yet everything that enters it falls into abatement, a parallel the Oxquarry commentary notes. Here the image is turned to bawdy argument: she is like the sea, and one more contribution will not overfill her. 'Still' again means always.

title: rich in 'Will,' add to thy 'Will'
short: She is rich in will (desire, lovers called Will), and should add his one will to make her store greater.
body: The language of wealth and addition (store, abundance, rich, add, more) makes desire a matter of accumulation, a cynical parody of the financial imagery of the procreation sonnets. Line 12, 'to make thy large will more', joins sexual and verbal excess: the sonnet's own piling-up of 'will' imitates the abundance it describes. The insistent repetition of a single word in shifting senses is a rhetorical figure (antanaclasis) that Elizabethan handbooks taught, here pushed to comic excess.

title: Let no unkind 'No' fair beseechers kill
short: Let no unkind refusal kill your fair suitors; the Quarto's punctuation allows other readings.
body: The Quarto reads 'Let no vnkinde, no faire beseechers kill', which editors have punctuated in different ways. The archive's text makes 'No' a noun, an unkind refusal. Other editors print 'Let no unkind, no fair beseechers kill', taking 'unkind' as a noun ('unkind one, kill no fair suitors') or as describing the suitors. The RPO edition glosses 'unkind' as describing the beseechers. 'Kill' plays on the Petrarchan convention that the lady's refusal slays her lover.

title: Think all but one, and me in that one 'Will'
short: Think all your lovers to be one single Will, and count me as part of that one.
body: The last line asks her to regard all her suitors as one (they are all 'Will', desire) and to include the poet in that single will. It can also be heard against the proverb 'one is no number', used in the next sonnet (136): one more makes no difference. The Oxquarry commentary also hears the idiom 'all's one' (it does not matter). The closing pun on the poet's own name makes the sonnet a signature, since the speaker is identified as Will.
